questions.q: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C? (specific heat capacity of water \(4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: The temperature rise is 70 − 20 = 50 K. \(Q = mc\Delta\theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 50 = 4.2 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}\). Using the final temperature in place of the rise is the usual slip.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C? (specific latent heat of fusion of ice \(3.3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(Q = ml = 0.40 \times 3.3 \times 10^{5} = 1.3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}\). There is no temperature term: the temperature stays at 0 °C while the ice melts.

questions.q: What is the internal energy of a body?

options.A: The sum of the randomly distributed kinetic and potential energies of its particles.
options.B: The total kinetic energy of the body as it moves.
options.C: The energy transferred to the body by heating.
options.D: The temperature of the body multiplied by its mass.

questions.solution: Internal energy is the total of the random kinetic energies and the potential energies of all the particles in the body. It can be raised by heating the body or by doing work on it.

questions.q: A solid is melting at constant temperature. What is happening to the energies of its particles?

options.A: Their kinetic energy and potential energy both increase.
options.B: Their kinetic energy increases and their potential energy stays the same.
options.D: Their kinetic energy stays the same and their potential energy increases.

questions.solution: Temperature measures the mean kinetic energy of the particles, and it is not changing. The energy supplied breaks bonds and moves particles apart, which raises their potential energy. So internal energy rises with no rise in temperature.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas at 100 kPa has a volume of 6.0 litres. It is compressed at constant temperature to 2.0 litres. What is its new pressure?
questions.solution: At constant temperature \(pV\) is constant (Boyle's law): 100 × 6.0 = p × 2.0, so p = 300 kPa. The volume has fallen to a third, so the pressure has trebled.

questions.q: A container of volume \(0.050\ \text{m}^{3}\) holds 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K. What is the pressure of the gas? (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(pV = nRT\), so \(p = \frac{nRT}{V} = \frac{2.0 \times 8.31 \times 300}{0.050} = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\). The temperature must be in kelvin.

questions.q: What is a temperature of 300 K in degrees Celsius?
questions.solution: A temperature in kelvin is the Celsius temperature plus 273. So the Celsius temperature is 300 − 273 = 27 °C. Adding 273 instead (573 °C) is the usual slip.

options.A: The temperature at which water freezes.
options.B: The lowest possible temperature, at which particles have their minimum kinetic energy.
options.C: The temperature at which all gases turn to liquid.
options.D: The temperature at which a gas has its greatest pressure.

questions.solution: Absolute zero, 0 K or −273 °C, is the lowest possible temperature. The particles have their minimum kinetic energy, and an ideal gas would exert no pressure.

questions.q: How many molecules are there in 0.50 mol of a gas? (\(N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: One mole contains the Avogadro constant of molecules. \(N = nN_{A} = 0.50 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 3.0 \times 10^{23}\).

questions.q: What is the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at 300 K? (\(k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: \(\frac{1}{2}m\langle c^{2}\rangle = \frac{3}{2}kT = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.2 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{J}\). It depends only on the temperature, not on which gas it is.

questions.q: The kelvin temperature of an ideal gas is doubled. What happens to the root mean square speed of its molecules?

options.A: It increases by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).
options.C: It increases by a factor of four.

questions.solution: Mean kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, and kinetic energy depends on speed squared. So the mean square speed doubles, and the root mean square speed rises by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.q: Which is not an assumption of the kinetic theory model of an ideal gas?

options.B: Collisions between molecules and with the walls are elastic.
options.C: The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
options.D: The molecules attract each other strongly between collisions.

questions.solution: The model assumes there are no forces between molecules except during collisions. It also assumes random motion, elastic collisions, molecules of negligible volume, and collisions that take a negligible time.

questions.q: A gas is heated in a sealed container of fixed volume. Why does its pressure rise?

options.A: The molecules move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with a greater change of momentum.
options.B: The molecules get bigger, so they take up more room.
options.C: There are more molecules in the container.

questions.solution: Pressure comes from molecules colliding with the walls and changing momentum. At a higher temperature they move faster: each collision has a larger change of momentum and collisions are more frequent. Both raise the force on the walls.

questions.q: Smoke particles in air are seen through a microscope to move in a random, jerky way. What does this Brownian motion show?

options.B: Air molecules are in rapid random motion.
options.D: Smoke particles are lighter than air molecules.

questions.solution: The smoke particles are knocked about by uneven bombardment from air molecules, which are too small to see. Their random, jerky paths are evidence that the air molecules are moving quickly and randomly.

questions.q: A gas expands by \(2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\) against a constant pressure of \(1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}\). How much work does the gas do?
questions.solution: At constant pressure, work done is pressure times change in volume: \(W = p\Delta V = 1.0 \times 10^{5} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\) = 200 J.

questions.q: A 50 W heater runs for 200 s and raises the temperature of a 0.50 kg metal block by 25 K. Assuming no energy is lost, what is the specific heat capacity of the metal?
questions.solution: Energy supplied: 50 × 200 = 10 000 J. Then \(c = \frac{Q}{m\Delta\theta} = \frac{10\,000}{0.50 \times 25} = 800\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\). In practice some energy is lost, so the measured value comes out too high.
